question:
Patient note:
A 36-year-old woman is evaluated in the pre-operative holding area of the general surgery ward in advance of a scheduled laparoscopic washout and adhesiolysis for a persistent left tubo-ovarian abscess that failed to resolve after a two-week course of broad-spectrum antibiotics; the procedure is expected to last approximately ninety minutes under general anaesthesia with carbon-dioxide insufflation and three port sites. She was admitted to hospital nineteen days ago with shaking chills, spiking temperatures to 40 °C, tachycardia in the 140s, and diffuse lower-abdominal pain; blood cultures at that time grew Escherichia coli, and serum lactate peaked at 4.1 mmol/L—findings consistent with septic physiology—prompting immediate fluid resuscitation, vasopressor support, and empiric meropenem. Her haemodynamics stabilised within 48 hours, but she has remained an inpatient because serial pelvic ultrasounds demonstrate a loculated 6-cm fluid collection that interventional radiology deemed inaccessible to percutaneous drainage. Early in the admission peripheral access became unreliable during repeated vasopressor titrations, so a triple-lumen internal-jugular catheter was placed on hospital day two and continues to be used for drug administration and daily blood draws; the insertion site is clean, the sutures are intact, and there is brisk blood return. Since admission she has been placed on strict bed rest except for nursing-assisted transfers to a bedside commode, accumulating fewer than 150 steps per day per the wearable device she kept on her wrist until battery exhaustion five days ago; physical therapy has not yet cleared her for ambulation because of light-headedness on attempted standing. She denies any operations, endoscopic procedures, or deliveries in the thirty days preceding this hospital stay, and the last time she was in an operating theatre was six years ago for an uncomplicated caesarean section. Past medical history is otherwise unremarkable—she has never been told she has heart-failure exacerbations, chronic lung disease, inflammatory bowel conditions, malignancy, or clotting disorders. She reports no prior fractures of the pelvis, hip, or long bones, no casting or splinting, no high-speed accidents, and no neurologic injuries that produced limb weakness or paralysis. There is no personal or first-degree family history of deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, or spontaneous miscarriages. She does not smoke, drinks wine once a month, and has never used hormonal contraception, selective oestrogen-receptor modulators, corticosteroids, or erythropoiesis-stimulating agents. Home medications before admission consisted solely of an over-the-counter multivitamin and occasional ibuprofen; inpatient orders currently include meropenem, intravenous fluids at maintenance rate, and daily folic-acid supplementation that haematology recommended after a hypercoagulability panel revealed fasting plasma homocysteine of 19 µmol/L, while tests for antiphospholipid antibodies and platelet-factor-4 complexes were negative. Review of systems today is negative for cough, sputum production, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, chest pressure, palpitations, focal neurological deficits, calf pain, ankle swelling, or dyspnoea at rest. On examination she lies supine at 20° head elevation, appears fatigued but cooperative, and converses in full sentences. Vital signs recorded ten minutes ago show temperature 37.2 °C, blood pressure 112/68 mm Hg, heart rate 92 beats per minute in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 16 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 % on room air, and body-mass index 25 kg/m². Jugular venous contour is not distended, carotid upstrokes are brisk, heart sounds are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and lungs are clear bilaterally with good aeration. Abdomen is soft but mildly distended; palpation elicits moderate tenderness in the left lower quadrant without rebound or guarding, and bowel sounds are present. Inspection of both lower extremities shows warm, well-perfused skin with no varicosities, pigmentation changes, or pitting oedema; calf circumferences measure 34 cm symmetrically, and gentle dorsiflexion causes no discomfort. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable 2 + bilaterally. Neurologic screening reveals intact cranial nerves, full strength in upper limbs, normal sensation to light touch and pinprick, and physiologic reflexes. The central-line dressing over the right neck is dry and transparent, and no erythema or induration tracks along the catheter tunnel. Morning laboratory studies drawn from the distal lumen demonstrate haemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, haematocrit 38 %, platelet count 243 × 10⁹/L, white-cell count 7.4 × 10⁹/L with a normal differential, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 0.84 mg/dL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 24 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.1 s with an international normalised ratio of 1.0, activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s, and a repeat homocysteine that remains elevated at 18 µmol/L despite supplementation. A 12-lead electrocardiogram reviewed by anaesthesia shows normal sinus rhythm at 88 beats per minute with no conduction delays or ischaemic changes. An upright chest radiograph obtained yesterday confirms correct central-line tip position at the cavo-atrial junction, clear lung fields, and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette. Ultrasound Doppler of both femoral and popliteal veins performed five days ago as part of fever work-up showed compressibility throughout. She has been nil per mouth since midnight; sequential compression sleeves are fitted around both calves but remain off until induction, and no anticoagulant prophylaxis has yet been started pending final peri-operative planning.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The preoperative Caprini VTE score assigns points for the planned procedure and for patient-specific thrombotic risk factors. At age 36 she gets 0 age points; BMI 25 does not exceed the >25 threshold (0).
Planned laparoscopic surgery lasting 90 minutes (>45 minutes): +2. Bed rest for 19 days (>72 hours): +2. Current internal-jugular central venous catheter: +2. Elevated homocysteine (18–19 µmol/L): +3. These factors sum to 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 9.
There is a discrepancy: sepsis 19 days ago also meets the Caprini criterion of sepsis within 1 month (+1), even though hemodynamics have stabilized. Thus the full score supported by the note is 9 + 1 = 10; 9 is the subtotal obtained by omitting recent sepsis.
Final answer: 9
